title: Free time
description: Hobbies with gern, lieber and am liebsten, how often you do things, verb-second word order in full, and making plans with friends.

grammarNotes.title: gern, lieber, am liebsten
grammarNotes.body:
To say you **like doing** something, take the verb and add **gern** (literally *gladly*). There's no separate *like* verb: *gern* goes right after the verb, or after *du* in a question.

- *Ich spiele **gern** Tennis.* = I like playing tennis.
- *Spielst du **gern** Tennis?* = Do you like playing tennis?
- *Ich tanze **nicht gern**.* = I don't like dancing. (*nicht so gern* = not that keen)

To compare, use **lieber** (rather, prefer) and **am liebsten** (most of all), like *good, better, best*. *am liebsten* often comes first, so the verb comes straight after it: ***Am liebsten** lese ich.*

You'll also hear **gerne**: it means exactly the same.
table: Most of all I like reading.

grammarNotes.title: Verb second: anything can go first
grammarNotes.body:
In a German statement, the verb with the ending is always the **second item**. Usually the subject comes first, but almost anything can take position 1: a time, a place, a *how often* word, even the object. The verb stays in position 2, and the subject moves to just **after** the verb.

- Count *items*, not words: *am Wochenende* is one item.
- *und*, *aber* and a *Ja,* or *Nein,* at the start don't count: *Ja, am Sonntag **habe** ich Zeit.*
- Separable prefixes and second verbs still go to the **end**: *Abends sehe ich **fern**. Morgen muss ich **arbeiten**.*

In a **yes/no question**, position 1 stays empty and the verb comes **first**: *Spielst du gern Fußball?* In a **W-question**, the question word takes position 1: *Was machst du?*

grammarNotes.title: lesen, sehen, treffen: vowel changes
grammarNotes.body:
Some common verbs change their vowel in the **du** and **er / sie / es** forms only. All the other forms are regular.

- **e → ie**: *lesen → du liest*, *sehen → er sieht* (just like *fernsehen*)
- **e → i**: *treffen → du triffst, er trifft* (just like *sprechen* and *essen*)

*du liest* has only one *s*, because the stem *les-* already ends in an *s* sound.

grammarNotes.title: How often? immer, oft, manchmal, nie
grammarNotes.body:
These words say how often you do something. They usually go right **after the verb**: *Ich lese **oft**.* In a question or after inversion, they come after the subject: *Liest du **oft**?*

You can also put one first. The verb is still second: ***Manchmal** singe ich.*

**nie** already means *not ever*, so never add *nicht* to it: *Ich tanze nie.* = I never dance.
table: Ich stehe immer um sieben Uhr auf.
I always get up at seven.

grammarNotes.title: Making plans
grammarNotes.body:
Learn these as chunks.

**Gehen wir …?** and **Wollen wir …?** both mean *Shall we …?* The verb comes first, then *wir*. With *wollen*, the second verb goes to the end: *Wollen wir zusammen **wandern**?*

**ins Kino** = to the cinema. Just learn it as a chunk for now: *Ich gehe gern ins Kino.*

**die Lust** is the wish to do something: *Hast du Lust?* = Do you feel like it? *Ich habe keine Lust.* = I don't feel like it.
table: Gehen wir ins Kino? / Wollen wir zusammen schwimmen?
Ich habe leider keine Zeit. / Ich habe keine Lust.

exercises.title: Freizeit and Hobbys
exercises.body:
- **die Freizeit** = free time (*frei* = free + *die Zeit* = time)
- **das Hobby** = the hobby, plural **die Hobbys**, just like English

To ask a friend: **Was sind deine Hobbys?**

You'll also hear **Was machst du in deiner Freizeit?** (What do you do in your free time?) Learn it as a chunk for now.

examples.translation: I have free time at the weekend.

examples.text: Was machst du in deiner Freizeit?
examples.translation: What do you do in your free time?

exercises.title: spielen: to play
exercises.body:
**spielen** = to play, a regular verb: ich spiele, du spielst, er spielt. The *sp* at the start sounds like *shp*.

Use it for games and ball sports:

- **der Fußball** = football (soccer)
- **das Tennis** = tennis

No article needed: *Ich spiele Fußball.* = I play football.

accepted: spielt
exercises.translation: He plays tennis.
We're playing football on Saturday.

exercises.title: Sport machen, Musik hören
exercises.body:
- **der Sport** = sport. In German you *make* sport: **Sport machen** = to do sport, to exercise.
- **die Musik** = music. Stress the end: *moo-ZEEK*.
- **hören** = to hear, to listen to. **Musik hören** = to listen to music. No extra word for *to*!

exercises.title: gern: liking to do something
exercises.body:
To say you **like doing** something, take the verb and add **gern** right after it:

- *Ich spiele Fußball.* = I play football.
- *Ich spiele **gern** Fußball.* = I like playing football.

There's no separate verb for *like* here: **gern** (literally *gladly*) does the job. In a question it comes after *du*: *Spielst du **gern** Tennis?*

You'll also hear **gerne**. It means exactly the same.

accepted: gern

exercises.title: Dance, swim, sing, hike
exercises.body:
Four more regular verbs:

- **tanzen** = to dance
- **schwimmen** = to swim
- **singen** = to sing
- **wandern** = to hike, to go walking in the countryside

Two small things: *tanzen* already ends in an *s* sound, so it's just du **tanzt**. And *wandern* keeps its *e* for *ich*: ich **wandere**, du wanderst, er wandert.

exercises.translation: Do you like swimming? (informal)

exercises.title: nicht gern
exercises.body:
Don't like it? Put **nicht** before *gern*:

- *Ich tanze **nicht gern**.* = I don't like dancing.
- *Ich schwimme **nicht so gern**.* = I'm not that keen on swimming.

*nicht so gern* is softer, and very common.

examples.translation: I'm not that keen on swimming.

exercises.instruction: A friend asks you this. You love singing. What do you say?

exercises.title: lieber and am liebsten
exercises.body:
*gern* has two bigger forms, just like *good, better, best*:

- **gern** = like doing
- **lieber** = prefer doing, would rather
- **am liebsten** = like doing most of all

*Ich schwimme gern, aber ich tanze **lieber**.* = I like swimming, but I prefer dancing.

**am liebsten** often goes first. The verb stays **second**, so *ich* moves after it: ***Am liebsten** tanze ich.*

exercises.title: lesen: e changes to ie
exercises.body:
**lesen** = to read. Like *fernsehen*, it changes **e → ie** in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms:

- ich lese
- du **liest**
- er / sie **liest**
- wir / sie / Sie lesen

*du liest* has only one *s*: the stem already ends in *s*.

**das Buch** = the book, plural **die Bücher**.

mouthShapes.caption: Bücher: say ee, then round your lips

accepted: liest
exercises.translation: He's reading a book.

exercises.title: sehen: to see, to watch
exercises.body:
**sehen** = to see, to watch. You know it from *fernsehen*, and it changes the same way: du **siehst**, er / sie **sieht**. The *h* is silent: *ZAY-en*.

**der Film** = the film, plural **die Filme**. It's a *der* word, so as an object it becomes **einen Film**, as you learned in Unit 5.

examples.translation: Tom watches a film in the evening.

accepted: sieht
exercises.translation: Tom is watching a film.

exercises.title: treffen: e changes to i
exercises.body:
**treffen** = to meet (when you've arranged it). It changes **e → i**, like *sprechen* and *essen*:

- ich treffe
- du **triffst**
- er / sie **trifft**
- wir / sie / Sie treffen

The person you meet is the object, so *mein* becomes **meinen** for a *der* word: *Ich treffe **meinen** Bruder.*

examples.text: Er trifft am Samstag seinen Bruder.
examples.translation: He's meeting his brother on Saturday.

accepted: trifft

exercises.title: Verb second, always
exercises.body:
You've seen that you can start with a time, and then the subject moves after the verb. Here's the full rule:

**Almost anything** can go first: a time, a place, even the object. Whatever comes first, the verb stays in **position 2**, and the subject comes **right after it**.

- *Ich spiele am Wochenende Tennis.*
- ***Am Wochenende** spiele ich Tennis.*
- ***Tennis** spiele ich am Wochenende.*

All three mean *I play tennis at the weekend*. Whatever you put first gets a little extra weight.

examples.translation: I play tennis at the weekend.
At the weekend I play tennis.
Tennis is what I play at the weekend.

exercises.prompt: At the weekend I play tennis.

exercises.translation: On Sunday we play football. (start with the day)

exercises.title: How often? oft, manchmal, nie
exercises.body:
- **immer** = always (you know this one)
- **oft** = often
- **manchmal** = sometimes
- **nie** = never

Put them right after the verb: *Ich lese **oft**. Er tanzt **nie**.*

Or put one first, and the verb is still second: ***Manchmal** singe ich.*

examples.translation: We always go hiking on Sunday.

accepted: Oft
exercises.translation: I often read in the evening.

exercises.title: Starting with a place or an object
exercises.body:
A place can go first too: ***Hier** spielen wir Fußball.*

You can even start with the object, to stress it or contrast it: ***Fußball** spiele ich nie, aber **Tennis** spiele ich oft.*

Count *items*, not words: *am Wochenende* or *in Berlin* is one item. And *und* and *aber* don't count at all: *…, aber **am liebsten** lese ich.*

examples.translation: Football is something I don't like playing.

exercises.title: Questions: verb first
exercises.body:
In a yes/no question, nothing comes before the verb. The verb goes **first**, then the subject:

- *Du spielst gern Fußball.* (statement)
- ***Spielst** du gern Fußball?* (question)

W-questions follow the verb-second rule: the question word takes position 1, the verb comes next. ***Was** machst du am Wochenende?*

exercises.translation: Do you often play tennis? (informal)

exercises.title: Making plans
exercises.body:
- **Gehen wir ins Kino?** = Shall we go to the cinema? Verb first, then *wir*. **ins Kino** = to the cinema; learn it as a chunk.
- **Wollen wir …?** = Shall we …? The second verb goes to the end: *Wollen wir **zusammen** wandern?* (**zusammen** = together)
- **Hast du Lust?** = Do you feel like it? **die Lust** is the wish to do something. **Ich habe keine Lust.** = I don't feel like it.
- **Ja, gern!** = Yes, I'd love to! **Gute Idee!** = Good idea!
- **das Konzert** = the concert, said *kon-TSERT*

examples.text: Gehen wir am Freitag ins Kino?
examples.translation: Shall we go to the cinema on Friday?
Sorry, I don't feel like it.
